A wheat plant that has just borne fruit; compare 来
Pictograph of wheat. The current meaning "come" is a phonetic loan. The original meaning "wheat" is now written as 麥.
周所受瑞麥來麰。一來二縫，象芒朿之形。天所來也，故爲行來之來。《詩》曰：“詒我來麰。”凡來之屬皆从來。

Pictogram (象形) of wheat – original character of 麥 (OC *mrɯːɡ, “wheat”) or 麳 (OC *rɯː, “wheat”). The line in the middle represents the ear, the two lines pointing upwards represent leaves, and the lines pointing downwards represent the stem and roots. An additional horizontal line was often added at the top end of the character, possibly used to emphasize the ear of the wheat. Compare 禾; both are unrelated to 釆.
This character has been borrowed for “to come” since the oracle bone script. During the Western Zhou and Warring States periods, additional semantic components, such as 止 (“foot”) or 辵 (“to walk”), were added to differentiate the original sense from the borrowed sense. However, these additions were not inherited in later scripts.
Some consider the derivative 麥 from the addition of 夊 (“to walk slowly”) to be the original form for the meaning “to come”. If so, their meanings have interchanged due to frequent use of 來 for “to come”.
Shuowen connects “wheat” and “to come” from a mythological standpoint: 天所來也 (“it comes from the heavens”). This may be supported by archaeological evidence, which suggests that wheat is not native to China, but originated in the Fertile Crescent.
來 and 麥 have both been reconstructed to begin with *mr- in Old Chinese. The former retains the liquid as /l/, while the latter retains the nasal /m/.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *la-j ~ ra (“to come”) (STEDT). Cognate with 迨 (OC *l'ɯːʔ, “to reach; until”), 賚 (OC *rɯːs, “to bestow”), Burmese လာ (la, “to come”). Also cognate with 蒞 (OC *rɯbs, “to arrive”) according to Schuessler (2007). Unclear if connected to Vietnamese lại (“come; again”).
Cognate to or same word as 麥 (OC *mrɯːɡ) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.field: 說文解字·來; 說文解字注
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry explains 來 as a auspicious wheat received by Zhou, describes the form as resembling wheat awns, and says it was then used for the sense ‘come’. The later Shuowen commentary argues that the graph’s original wheat sense was extended to things arriving, while noting that this account implies a Zhou-origin chronology it cannot confirm. This is a historical lexicographic explanation, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest use.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

evidence.field: 字源字形; cited oracle-bone and bronze inscription records
evidence.text: The page lists 52 oracle-bone examples and 13 bronze-inscription examples, including late Shang and early Western Zhou vessel records, and displays a script-stage sequence through bronze, Chu manuscripts, seal, Qin slips, and clerical script. It supports a long graphic record and later standardization, but text extraction alone does not establish which visible stroke in each ancient form depicts a particular botanical part.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

evidence.field: 基本解釋; 來 lái senses
evidence.text: The dictionary separately records ‘wheat’ with Shuowen and Book of Odes citations, and ‘come/arrive’ with citations from Erya and Analects. It also lists later extensions including submit, attract, arise, future, past, and grammatical uses. These entries document attested senses but their list order is not a semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Book of Poetry, Si Wen
evidence.text: The poem contains ‘貽我來牟、帝命率育’ (‘bestowed wheat and barley, appointed by Heaven for nourishment’ in the linked Legge translation). The text gives an early literary attestation for 來牟 as grain terminology, but does not independently date the poem’s composition or resolve whether 來 alone names wheat in the phrase.
evidence.title: 詩經 : 頌 : 周頌 : 清廟之什 : 思文

evidence.field: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction, publication and methodology description
evidence.text: Baxter and Sagart’s 2014 book presents a reconstruction of Old Chinese drawing on archaic dialect documentation, early loan layers, excavated manuscripts and derivational relationships. The public page establishes the reconstruction work’s authorship, date, and general method, but does not expose the character-specific entries needed here to confirm individual forms.
evidence.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction

evidence.text: The inspected local TSV includes the two 來 rows above, but no 麥 row was found using the searched character key. The official Baxter–Sagart table lists 麥 separately as *m-rˤəkә (dialect: *m-rˤ > *mˤr-) ‘wheat’. This spelling is not identical to 來’s *mə.rˤək; the same broad correspondence is apparent, but the exact forms should not be silently normalized or represented as identical.

evidence.text: The dictionary classifies 来 as a variant of 來 and cites historical clerical and stele forms, including later graphic deformation. It supports a nonchronological variant relation rather than establishing that 来 was officially standardized as the simplified form.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A00138 entry, Shuowen and form notes
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the Shuowen explanation: Zhou received auspicious wheat called 來麰; the graph resembles awned wheat and was used for ‘come’. It describes the seal form as wheat-like, but this is a historical dictionary account, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest referent or of a Zhou-origin date.
evidence.title: A00138 來 - Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.field: Article note 65, graph relationship of 來 and 麥
evidence.text: The article presents the common account: 來 is a plant-shaped graph originally used for wheat; adding a foot element produced 麥 for ‘wheat’ while 來 was borrowed for ‘come’, attributed to sound similarity. It also describes the proposals as an inference, and points out interpretive difficulties in reading grain contexts in the Odes. This supports a conventional analysis, not certainty about pre-Shang graph origin or the original spoken name of the depicted plant.
evidence.title: Ji 姬 and Jiang 姜: The Role of Exogamic Clans in the Organization of the Zhou Polity

evidence.field: Old Chinese table, U+4F86 and U+9EA5
evidence.text: The table lists 來 ‘come’ as *mə.rˤək (> *rˤə) and a kind of wheat as *mə.rˤək (> *mə.rˤə); 麥 ‘wheat’ is listed separately as *m-rˤəkә (dialect: *m-rˤ > *mˤr-). This supports a historically related sound shape for the proposed whole-graph loan, while leaving the loan analysis itself an etymological interpretation rather than proof based solely on reconstruction.
evidence.title: BaxterSagartOCbyRadStr2014-09-20

evidence.field: Basic senses and cited classical examples
evidence.text: The entry separately lists wheat and ‘come/arrive’, citing Shuowen and the Odes for grain terminology and Erya and Analects for ‘come’. It also documents later uses such as return, submit/attract, arise, future, past, and grammatical functions. This is evidence for attested lexical uses as represented by the dictionary; its gloss order is not a chronology, and it does not establish a continuous semantic chain.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

evidence.field: Oracle bone, bronze, manuscript and later form catalogue
evidence.text: The entry records 52 oracle-bone examples, 13 bronze examples, Chu manuscript forms, seal, Qin slip and clerical examples. It reports late Shang and early Western Zhou material, documenting an early graphic record and later forms; the text listing alone does not show exact stroke-by-stroke transitions or securely date the first semantic use.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

evidence.field: Article on 來 and 麥, graph description and oracle-bone usages
evidence.text: The article describes late Shang oracle-bone and bronze 來 as a plant-shaped graph, with a stem, paired slanting leaves, and an upper ear-like part; it notes the upper extra mark may be an ear detail or ornamental stroke. It reports oracle-bone contexts using 來 predominantly for ‘come/go’, tribute, future year, and a place name, and argues the added foot graph 麥 was intended to mark the wheat word. This modern scholarly account gives contextual examples but does not independently establish a dated earliest occurrence of the wheat sense.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「來」與「麥」和中國小麥的身世之謎

evidence.text: The article is dated 2023-06-07 and discusses archaeological estimates for wheat transmission to China in the late Neolithic, with routes still debated. This makes external introduction of wheat a possible historical context for the Shuowen ‘came from Heaven’ story, but botanical diffusion does not prove the graph’s etymology or semantic motivation.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「來」與「麥」和中國小麥的身世之謎

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), quoting Duan Yucai’s Shuowen commentary
evidence.text: Duan interprets the grain ‘來麰’ as arriving from Heaven and explains extension to things that arrive. He explicitly remarks that this account would imply 來 first existed only at the beginning of Zhou, whose import is unclear. This traditional analysis conflicts in emphasis with the usual phonetic-loan account and cannot settle chronology.
evidence.title: 來 lái、lài - 漢典

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.
